entry.title: A systematic review of fifty studies maps fairness, accountability, transparency and ethics gaps in learning analytics
entry.summary:
A systematic mapping of fifty studies examined how the FATE principles, fairness, accountability, transparency and ethics, are built into learning analytics systems, identifying the tools used, the main ethical and technical challenges, and the stakeholders most affected. The review concludes that ethical practice can support a more equitable use of educational data, and that adopting these systems well requires governance structures and regular audits, with closer attention to the needs of under-represented student populations.

Why it matters here: PASS is itself a predictive model built on anonymised Wits School of Education data, so this review's own FATE checklist, governance, audits and attention to under-represented groups, is a direct test to run against the project's data pipeline and any dashboard, before a model's output reaches the School or its Business Intelligence Services.

Oliveira, Matos, Rodrigues, Lima and Lima, Revista Brasileira de Informática na Educação, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Revista Brasileira de Informática na Educação), systematic literature review

entry.title: A proposed ten-indicator early warning system for Argentina's higher education dropout, built on the OREALC/UNESCO model
entry.summary:
Pointing to Argentina's wide gap between students who enrol, stay and graduate from higher education, this paper designs an early warning system in three stages: identifying dropout risk factors, improving the use of administrative data and management information systems, and defining alert indicators. It sets out ten indicators structured under the Context-Input-Process-Product model used by UNESCO's regional office OREALC, intended to help institutions detect risk early and ground their own intervention strategies, though the paper presents a design rather than a system already evaluated in use.

Why it matters here: The OREALC/UNESCO Context-Input-Process-Product structure behind these ten indicators offers PASS a tested, non-technical frame for organising whatever risk indicators the Wits and Emory model ultimately produces, useful alongside the statistical model itself when the project explains its indicators to the School of Education or its Business Intelligence Services.

Cuttica, Gestión de la Educación, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Gestión de la Educación, Universidad de Costa Rica)

entry.title: An early-alert dashboard tracks every undergraduate's engagement and reaches out by text and email
entry.summary:
The University of Canterbury's Analytics for Course Engagement (ACE) programme began in early 2020 for first-year students and was extended to all undergraduates in 2021. It combines a student's activity on the LEARN (Moodle) platform and Echo360 lecture recordings into an engagement score, shown to the student on their own dashboard against the course average; when engagement drops during term time the student receives a personalised text message and email, and support teams, including first-year advisors, faculties, Student Accessibility, Halls, Student Care and the Māori and Pasifika Student Support teams, may follow up. The university states that ACE does not track lecture attendance or academic performance and is never used to assess students; the programme won the 2021 CAUDIT award for Improving Student Success.

Why it matters here: ACE is a working example, at full university scale, of the step PASS has not yet reached: turning a predictive signal into a named outreach workflow. Its declared limits, no use of attendance or grades and no assessment of students, are a useful boundary for Wits' Business Intelligence Services to weigh when PASS moves from an anonymised model to contact with real students.

University of Canterbury, Analytics for Course Engagement (ACE) programme · University programme page describing an operating institutional system, not independently peer-reviewed

entry.title: A proposed "LEAGUE" framework argues that legal compliance alone cannot make student-data analytics fair or accountable
entry.summary:
Sahana Varadaraju and Bharathwaj Vijayakumar of Rowan University argue that learning-analytics governance in higher education has stayed "compliance-first", centred on meeting baseline legal requirements such as the United States' FERPA and the European Union's GDPR, which they say does not by itself resolve questions of fairness, student agency, accountability or educational purpose. They propose the LEAGUE framework, a six-pillar model (Lawfulness, Equity, Agency, Governance, Utility and Ethics by Design) built from a conceptual synthesis of learning-analytics, educational-data-mining, data-ethics and educational-policy scholarship, and illustrate it with an early-alert case study.

Why it matters here: As PASS moves from building predictive models to co-creating interventions with the University's Business Intelligence Services, this framework offers a structured checklist, beyond mere compliance with South Africa's POPIA, for whether an early-alert intervention is fair, transparent and respects students' agency, not only whether it is legally permitted.

Varadaraju, S. and Vijayakumar, B., Rowan University, EDULEARN26 Proceedings (IATED), 2026 · Peer-reviewed conference paper (EDULEARN26 proceedings), author manuscript on arXiv, open access

entry.title: A survey experiment finds that a few targeted questions about motivation and degree-completion expectations predict university dropout better than personality measures
entry.summary:
Economists at CNRS and IESEG School of Management (Lille), and at Aarhus University, ran a survey experiment with incoming first-year students, linked to long-run administrative outcomes, to see which information improves dropout prediction beyond standard university records. They found that a small number of targeted, study-specific survey items, especially about motivation and expectations of degree completion, substantially improved predictive performance, while widely used measures of general traits such as grit and self-control added little, a result the authors say they qualitatively replicated in a large population.

Why it matters here: This offers the PASS team a concrete, low-cost addition to test alongside its anonymised Wits School of Education data: a handful of motivation and expectation questions rather than a full personality battery, which the authors report adds little once administrative records are already in the model. It is also a useful caution against assuming established psychological scales will automatically strengthen a predictive model.

Epper, T. F., Ibsen, K., Koch, A. K. and Nafziger, J., IZA Discussion Paper No. 18439, March 2026 · IZA working paper (discussion paper series), not yet peer-reviewed

entry.title: A randomised Dutch field experiment finds that an accurate early-warning system did not, by itself, reduce first-year dropout
entry.summary:
Researchers at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam ran a randomised field experiment at a large Dutch university to test whether an early-warning system, used by student counsellors to flag at-risk students for early intervention, reduced first-year dropout. The early-warning system accurately predicted which students were at risk, but the counselling it triggered did not reduce dropout or improve academic performance. The authors suggest that addressing poor academic performance may need more actionable feedback and better-targeted counselling practices than the warning alone provided.

Why it matters here: This is the clearest caution available to the PASS team that an accurate predictive model is not enough on its own: identifying at-risk Wits School of Education students correctly will not improve their outcomes unless the interventions that follow are themselves effective, a question PASS's co-creation work with the University's Business Intelligence Services will need to test directly rather than assume.

Plak, S., Cornelisz, I., Meeter, M. and van Klaveren, C., Higher Education Quarterly, 2022 · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Simplest model wins: comparing four algorithms for predicting student attrition at a Kenyan university
entry.summary:
A study at the Technical University of Mombasa compared Logistic Regression, Decision Trees, Random Forest and Naive Bayes for predicting student attrition from a Kenyan university dataset gathered through a student questionnaire, using accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score and ROC-AUC as evaluation criteria. Logistic Regression performed best, reaching 56.67% accuracy and a ROC-AUC of 0.60, while Decision Trees and Random Forest each started at 40% accuracy, with Random Forest improving to 52% after hyperparameter tuning, and Naive Bayes reached 46.67% accuracy with a balanced F1 score of 0.47.

Why it matters here: The study is a useful methodological comparison for PASS because it tests the same shortlist of classical algorithms, Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Decision Trees and Naive Bayes, on a Kenyan university's own student data rather than an imported dataset, and finds that the simplest model can still outperform ensemble methods when a dataset is modest in size. Its modest accuracy scores are also a reminder that PASS should expect, and report honestly, model performance that may fall well short of figures obtained on larger or more established datasets until the Wits School of Education's own records grow.

Nyawira, Musau, Adem and Jobunga, Journal of the Kenya National Commission for UNESCO, 2025 · Academic journal article (Journal of the Kenya National Commission for UNESCO), open access

entry.title: No evidence dashboards lift grades: a systematic review of 38 learning-analytics studies
entry.summary:
A systematic and quantitative review of 38 research studies on learning analytics dashboards found no evidence to support the claim that they have improved students' academic achievement, with most individual studies reporting negligible or small effects and few well-powered controlled experiments among them. The review found a relatively substantial effect of dashboards on student participation, with several studies reporting medium to large effect sizes, but only modest and inconsistent effects on motivation and attitudes, and it identified recurring weaknesses such as comparing dashboard users with non-users instead of randomising, assuming that access equates to use, and a lack of standardised outcome measures.

Why it matters here: This review is a direct caution for PASS: a model that correctly flags at-risk students will not by itself raise achievement unless the dashboard built on it, and the interventions that follow, are evaluated with a properly controlled design rather than by simply comparing students who engage with it to those who do not. Before Emory and Wits report any effect of a PASS dashboard to the Wits School of Education or its Business Intelligence Services, the review's own list of recurring design weaknesses is a checklist worth testing the evaluation against.

Kaliisa, Misiejuk, López-Pernas, Khalil and Saqr, LAK '24 (ACM), 2024 · Peer-reviewed conference paper (ACM Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference, LAK '24), Best Full Paper award

entry.title: Weak at enrolment, strong after first grades: predicting dropout risk across eight Chilean universities
entry.summary:
Drawing on data from eight Chilean universities, the study found that information available at the point of matriculation only weakly predicted whether a student would persist, while the model's predictive power improved markedly once first university grades became available. Financial aid predicted higher persistence and being denied a student's first-choice major predicted lower persistence, and the authors found that student success programmes were effective at some universities and ineffective at others, often failing even where effective to reach the highest-risk students.

Why it matters here: This is a close precedent for PASS's own staged approach, since it shows that a predictive model's power grows chiefly once in-programme performance data, not just admissions data, becomes available, so PASS should expect its earliest Wits School of Education models to sharpen after a first semester or year of local grades. It is also a caution that identifying at-risk students is not enough on its own: PASS's interventions, co-created with the University's Business Intelligence Services, will need checking that they reach the highest-risk students and not only the easiest to help.

Von Hippel and Hofflinger, Journal of Higher Education Policy and Management, 2021 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Journal of Higher Education Policy and Management, Taylor & Francis)

entry.title: Guanxi and the dual-teacher model as predictors: a hybrid Random Forest-Neural Network framework for Chinese student retention
entry.summary:
Researchers at City University, Malaysia propose a hybrid Random Forest-Neural Network model for predicting dropout and delayed graduation in Chinese undergraduate populations, combining demographic, academic, financial, psychological and institutional data with feature engineering and data-balancing methods. The authors report that academic failure, financial hardship, mental health problems and practical difficulties are the strongest predictors, and argue that adding culturally specific constructs, guanxi (social-network obligation), Confucian pedagogical structures and the dual-teacher model, improved how well the model fits Chinese higher-education settings.

Why it matters here: The paper is a reminder that a predictive model built on one country's assumptions about what predicts dropout may miss locally specific factors; before PASS extends beyond the Wits School of Education, the Emory-Wits team should ask what comparably specific South African or Global South constructs, language of instruction, extended-family financial obligation, distance from home, its own model may be missing.

Zhang and Chamran, International Journal of Academic Research in Business and Social Sciences, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article (International Journal of Academic Research in Business and Social Sciences), open access

entry.title: Built for a Ghanaian university, tested on open data: a PhD thesis reaches 92% accuracy on which students will not graduate
entry.summary:
A PhD thesis at South Africa's Durban University of Technology set out to predict which students at a Ghanaian higher education institution were at risk of not graduating, combining activity logs, course and demographic data and assessment records; in the absence of the Ghanaian institution's own data, the model was built and tested on the UK's Open University Learning Analytics Dataset. A Random Forest model outperformed gradient boosting, CatBoost, k-nearest neighbours, logistic regression and naive Bayes on accuracy, precision, recall and F1 score, and when trained only on the most useful features, assignment submission date, total clicks on learning activities, assessment score, registration date, credits studied and unregistration date, it reached 92% accuracy in less time than a model using every available feature.

Why it matters here: The thesis is a direct precedent for PASS's own plan to validate a predictive model on one dataset before it has enough local records: PASS can test the same shortlist of high-value features, submission timing, activity clicks, assessment scores, against its own Wits School of Education data once available, rather than waiting to build a full feature set first.

Tahiru, PhD thesis, Durban University of Technology, 2023 · PhD thesis (Durban University of Technology, Information Technology), institutional repository

entry.title: StudentAnalyse at Prague's Czech Technical University: first-year dropout nearly halved after a four-year early-warning rollout
entry.summary:
The Open University's OU Analyse predictive learning analytics research was adapted as StudentAnalyse for the Faculty of Mechanical Engineering at the Czech Technical University in Prague, which had a first-year drop-out rate averaging 37% before adopting it in 2015/16. Tutors used the system to flag at-risk students and apply intervention strategies; across the following four academic years, to 2018/19, the average drop-out rate fell to 19%, 422 more students progressed to second and third year, and the Vice-Dean reported about CZK 27.9 million (roughly GBP 950,000) in additional tuition income over that period.

Why it matters here: A single, tutor-facing risk dashboard sustained over several years, not a one-off model, is what took this faculty's drop-out rate down by half; it is the kind of multi-year institutional commitment PASS will need from the Wits School of Education's own Business Intelligence Services if an early model is to become a lasting intervention rather than a one-off pilot.

The Open University, Computing Research impact case study, "Using predictive learning analytics to improve student retention" · Institutional impact case study (The Open University), self-reported by the partner institutions

entry.title: Warning emails to students flagged as likely to drop out: no average effect at a German university, and responses that depend on who receives them
entry.summary:
Economists from the University of Wuppertal, the RWI Leibniz Institute for Economic Research and RH Köln evaluated a low-cost early alert system at a German university that emailed warnings to students whose predicted dropout probability was high. The average effect of the warnings was not statistically significant, but responses differed: previously active students, especially outside STEM, cut their exam registrations by up to two courses and modestly improved their grades, while inactive students did not respond and dropout probability rose slightly in structured programmes. The authors used causal forests to examine this variation and conclude that warnings must fit students' prior engagement, the structure of their programme and the timing of the intervention.

Why it matters here: This is the caution PASS needs before it hands risk scores to Wits: an accurate prediction does not by itself change outcomes, and a bare warning can even backfire for some students. Interventions co-created with Business Intelligence Services should therefore be tested for who responds, not only whether the average improves, and timed to the Wits School of Education's own programme structure.

Berens, Henao, Rumert and Schneider, Education Economics, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, published online ahead of issue (Taylor and Francis)

entry.title: Ireland tracks every new undergraduate through one national student record, and publishes progression and completion as an open dashboard
entry.summary:
Ireland's Higher Education Authority (HEA) reports progression, continuation and completion for full-time undergraduate new entrants at the institutions it funds, using the national Student Record System census that institutions return each 1 March, and publishes the results as an interactive dashboard that can be filtered by institution and field of study. Its 2026 release finds that 9.3% of 2023/24 new entrants neither progressed nor transferred to another institution, the lowest rate since 2019/20, ranging from 4.5% in Education to 18.8% in Services, with mature entrants at 13.4%. Of students who entered in 2019/20, 76.6% had completed a programme by 2024, with Education highest at 90.4%.

Why it matters here: The HEA dashboard shows what a shared, institution-level evidence base for progression looks like, with small cells suppressed to protect students, and its Education figures give PASS an outside benchmark for the Wits School of Education. Business Intelligence Services at Wits could adopt the same clear definitions of progressed, transferred and non-progressed students before any predictive model is trained.

Higher Education Authority, Ireland, news release by James Holohan, 9 July 2026 · Official national statistics from Ireland's higher education funding and policy agency

entry.title: Predicting dropout across Saudi universities from 4,560 students, with work, family and cultural factors alongside grades
entry.summary:
Researchers built dropout prediction models for Saudi universities that go beyond academic records to include personal, social and cultural factors, noting that national reports put non-completion among Saudi university students at 40% to 50% while few studies had looked across several institutions. Using data from 4,560 students and twelve feature-selection-based learning models, they found that a K-Nearest Neighbors model with Recursive Feature Elimination performed best, with an accuracy of 97.6%. SHAP and LIME explanations identified GPA, academic year, employment status, support from family and friends and prior knowledge of the major as the most influential features, and a formal evaluation framework found that LIME's explanations outperformed SHAP's on fidelity, local concordance, prescriptivity and stability.

Why it matters here: PASS can borrow the study's two-layer design: registry variables such as GPA and year of study, which Business Intelligence Services already hold for the Wits School of Education, plus survey items on employment and family support that registry data miss. Its near-perfect accuracy on a single dataset is also a reminder that PASS should validate its models on later cohorts before any model guides an intervention.

Albugami, Wali and Almagrabi, PeerJ Computer Science, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY 4.0)

entry.title: University of Sharjah builds an explainable dropout early-warning system from a decade of UAE STEM enrolment records
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Sharjah built an explainable machine-learning early-warning system to flag dropout risk among undergraduate STEM students in the MENA region, using longitudinal data from 6,798 students at a major UAE university spanning ten cohorts from 2010 to 2019. Of six classifiers tested on routine student information system records, XGBoost, Gradient Boosting Machine and Random Forest performed best, each reaching an AUC-ROC above 0.91 and an F1-score above 0.84, with withdrawn semesters, second-term credit load, academic probation history and mathematics and physics performance the strongest predictors. The authors applied SHAP analysis to make the model's predictions interpretable at both the whole-population and individual-student level, and note the system needs no external surveys or learning-management-system data, only data already held by the registrar.

Why it matters here: PASS can test the same combination the Sharjah team used, routine student-system records plus SHAP explainability, as a benchmark against models trained on anonymised Wits School of Education data, and borrow its use of withdrawn semesters and credit load as predictors that a Business Intelligence Services dataset is likely to hold too.

Al Hashmi, Zervopoulos, Elmehdi and Ozturk, Emerging Science Journal, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: Two advising algorithms built on the same state community college system send fewer at-risk Black students the extra help they need
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Virginia examined two prediction models, one for course completion and one for degree completion, built on system-wide administrative records from the Virginia Community College System covering 2007 to 2019. They found that if either model were used to target extra support at "at-risk" students, algorithmic bias would mean fewer marginal Black students received that support than White students, and that the size of the bias changed depending on whether "at-risk" was defined as the bottom decile or the bottom half of predicted scores. They trace part of the bias to the administrative data being less predictive of Black students' success than of White students' success, particularly for new students, and suggest that collecting more data could narrow the gap.

Why it matters here: A direct warning for PASS before any model goes near the University's Business Intelligence Services data: reporting one overall accuracy figure is not enough, the same model can send support to fewer at-risk Black or minoritised students depending only on how "at-risk" is defined, and the fix may be collecting more predictive data on under-served groups rather than adjusting the algorithm after the fact.

Bird, Castleman and Song, Journal of Policy Analysis and Management, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article (subscription access, Wiley)

entry.title: A simple decision tree built from two years of enrolment records flags dropout risk at a Malaysian private university
entry.summary:
Researchers at Universiti Utara Malaysia, working with Oman's Ministry of Education, extracted 7,706 student records from a Malaysian private university's database covering the 2018 to 2019 intake to test decision tree and logistic regression classifiers for predicting dropout. After testing several data partitions, decision tree variants and logistic regression imputation methods, they found a chi-square decision tree with two branches performed best, reaching 89.49 percent accuracy on an 80/20 train-test split, and the chosen model also identified the variables most useful for predicting dropout. The authors frame dropout as a threat to university enrolment, revenue and student wellbeing, and argue the model could help flag at-risk students early.

Why it matters here: A directly comparable scale and data type to PASS's own starting point: a single institution's own enrolment records, modest classifiers rather than deep learning, and a result, 89.49 percent accuracy from a simple decision tree, that sets a realistic early benchmark for what anonymised Wits School of Education data alone might achieve before Business Intelligence Services data is added.

Roslan, Mohd Jamil, Mohd Shaharanee and Sultan Alawi, Journal of Advanced Research in Applied Sciences and Engineering Technology, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY-NC 4.0)

entry.title: Four South African universities, 30 staff and a Big Data framework for retention: Fort Hare maps the data and ethics gaps
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Fort Hare interviewed 30 academic staff members across four South African public universities and analysed institutional retention reports, policy documents and strategic plans, using an interpretivist qualitative approach supported by Design Science. They found fragmented data systems, limited data literacy among staff and concerns about the ethical use of data, alongside a stated need for predictive analytics, integrated data systems and personalised support. From this they propose a Big Data framework meant to move universities from reactive to proactive retention management through ethical data governance, integrated data processing, predictive analytics and personalised interventions.

Why it matters here: This study names the obstacles PASS must work through with the University's Business Intelligence Services before any model reaches advisers: data spread across separate systems, staff unused to reading risk data and worries about its ethical use. Its framework offers a checklist for the governance and staff-capacity side of PASS, which a purely technical model would miss.

Mainoti and Piderit, South African Journal of Information Management, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY 4.0)

entry.title: Tokyo University of Technology builds an early-warning model meant to survive the move to a new academic year
entry.summary:
Researchers at Tokyo University of Technology note that Japan's declining birthrate is widening the spread of academic ability among university students, making it crucial to identify students at risk of academic failure early. They present an early-warning system, built on learning-management-system data, that combines data augmentation with a transfer-learning classification model drawing on Transformer and XGBoost, designed for small samples and for the shift in student data from one academic year to the next. The authors report that it achieved the best overall performance against a conventional predictive model, that its stability was confirmed with the hold-out method, and that all data were collected without identifiable information.

Why it matters here: A PASS model trained on past Wits School of Education cohorts will meet the same difficulty when it is applied to a new intake: small programme-level samples and student populations that shift from year to year. This study offers a method to borrow for checking that a PASS model still holds in the next academic year, and a reminder to work with non-identifiable data from the start.

Tan, She, Chen, Ohno and Kameda, Journal of Advanced Computational Intelligence and Intelligent Informatics, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Fuji Technology Press)

entry.title: Brazil's State University of Maringá tests enrolment-only dropout prediction at scale
entry.summary:
Researchers at the State University of Maringá in Brazil evaluated Decision Tree, Random Forest and XGBoost models against enrolment records for 66,820 undergraduate students across 45 programmes from 2002 to 2022. Using only static, enrolment-time variables and a temporal validation split to control information leakage, XGBoost reached a PR-AUC of 0.586 against a dropout prevalence of 0.364, about 1.6 times random performance. Accuracy fell when a model trained on older cohorts was tested on newer ones, a decline the authors attribute to calibration shift rather than worse risk ranking, which they show can be corrected by adjusting the decision threshold without retraining.

Why it matters here: PASS also starts from existing institutional records rather than new survey data, so this large, long-run Brazilian dataset is a useful comparator for how much predictive power enrolment-time variables alone can offer, and a reminder to monitor and recalibrate any Wits model as cohorts change from year to year.

Mincache, Catharin, Teixeira, Colanzi, da Costa and Feltrim, Technologies, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: Brazilian and Chilean universities flag at-risk students from weekly Moodle activity
entry.summary:
Building on the LANSE learning-analytics platform, researchers from universities in Brazil and Chile trained a CatBoost model on Moodle log data covering 567 student-course instances across 23 courses, using 25 engagement and access features with NSGA-II hyperparameter optimisation and ADASYN resampling. A single model trained on relative course-progression data outperformed separate week-by-week models, reaching an F1-score of 0.86, recall of 0.85, accuracy of 0.90 and an AUC of 0.95 for at-risk students by week 7. The study compared weekly against unified modelling strategies rather than reporting only one model's accuracy.

Why it matters here: PASS could trial a similar Moodle log-based, within-course early-warning layer alongside its enrolment-record models, since this shows that activity data collected automatically during a course can flag at-risk students well before final grades are available.

Marcolino, Porto, Primo, Targino, Ramos, Queiroga, Munoz and Cechinel, Scientific Reports, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Nature Scientific Reports), open access

entry.title: Italy's University of Catania predicts undergraduate dropout with XGBoost
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Catania built a dropout prediction model from five years of historical records covering 42,000 undergraduate students across the university's departments. They compared logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost and a neural network to classify students as continuing or dropping out, and XGBoost reached 97 percent accuracy, with random forest close behind at 94 percent. The underlying data remain the university's own property, restricted to its data analysis office.

Why it matters here: This shows how far accuracy can go with routine administrative records alone at university scale, a useful benchmark as PASS moves from its Wits School of Education pilot data towards models built with the University's Business Intelligence Services.

Miracula, Mazzeo Rinaldi and Giuffrida, LOD 2024 conference proceedings (Springer), 2025 · Peer-reviewed conference proceedings (Springer Lecture Notes in Computer Science)

entry.title: Predicting dropout from a secondary-teacher programme: five Graz cohorts, an admission test and university marks
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Graz built a stacked ensemble model on five cohorts that entered the secondary-teacher bachelor's programme between 2015 and 2019 (2,661 students, of whom 1,124 dropped out), using the TESAT admission test of cognitive and personality measures, demographics and GPA. Admission test and demographics alone reached a mean accuracy of 0.61 and an AUC of 0.62, GPA alone 0.74 and 0.76, and the two combined 0.76 and 0.77. The authors describe the ensemble as a black box and say richer data, such as school grades, are needed before it is used for intervention.

Why it matters here: This is the closest published match to the first setting of PASS: dropout prediction inside an initial teacher education programme. It suggests that university marks carry most of the signal while admission data add little, a result PASS can test on Wits School of Education records, and its caution about black-box models supports PASS's aim of interpretable models built with Business Intelligence Services.

Jud, Weissenbacher and Neubauer, European Journal of Teacher Education, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)

entry.title: Forecasting next semester's results for 3,093 Ghanaian graduates across 14 degree programmes
entry.summary:
Using anonymised records of 3,093 graduates from the 2015 to 2019 intakes of a public university in Ghana, covering 14 four-year degree programmes and 40 features, the authors predicted each semester's GPA and class from the record up to the previous semester with Random Forest, SVM, LSTM and BiLSTM models. BiLSTM performed best, with classification accuracy rising from 58% in semester 2 to 62% in semester 8, and high-school grades and earlier semester GPAs were the strongest predictors. Because students who dropped out were excluded, the study predicts performance rather than dropout, and its accuracy is modest.

Why it matters here: An African, multi-programme case close to the PASS aim of spotting students likely to take longer to graduate: semester-by-semester forecasting from routine records is a design PASS could compare with one-off dropout models. Its exclusion of dropouts and modest accuracy also show why PASS needs data on students who leave, not only on those who finish.

Diekuu, Mekala, Abonie, Isaacs and Elyan, Cogent Education, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: Two simple triggers in weeks 3 and 4: how Charles Sturt reaches disengaged first-years before census
entry.summary:
In semester 1 of 2022 Charles Sturt University monitored 191 first-year units with 15,034 enrolments and, in weeks 3 and 4, flagged students who had not submitted an early low-stakes assessment or showed low activity on the learning platform; an Outreach Team contacted 1,386 flagged students by phone, two-way SMS and other channels. After contact 52% submitted the early assessment, 28% of those contacted came from low socioeconomic backgrounds against 22% across the university, and after a successful conversation retention into the next semester ranged from 64% for students with no equity factors to 75% for those with four or more. The authors note that there was no randomised control group.

Why it matters here: A working model for the intervention side of PASS: explainable triggers that advisers and students can understand, tied to a staffed outreach team and timed before the census date. The Wits team and Business Intelligence Services could adapt it for first-year students in the Wits School of Education and evaluate it with the comparison group this study lacked.

Linden, van der Ploeg and Roman, Journal of Higher Education Policy and Management, 2023 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (evaluation of an institutional programme)

entry.title: Mining Moodle logs in Baltic design courses to catch students about to drop out
entry.summary:
A researcher working with TTK University of Applied Sciences in Estonia and Vilnius Gediminas Technical University in Lithuania analysed 99,104 Moodle activity records from 154 students across six computer-aided design (CAD) courses, focusing on 12,941 logs from 80 students in the two courses with the highest attrition. A random forest model built on a new weighted attribute method, combining engagement, task difficulty and time allocation, reached a cross-validated accuracy of 0.8756, though the author describes the findings as preliminary given the small dataset and calls for external validation.

Why it matters here: Its explicit weighting of time-on-task and task difficulty alongside engagement, drawn straight from Moodle logs, is a practical feature-engineering idea PASS could test on the Wits School of Education's own learning management system data, and its honesty about small-sample limits is a useful caution for early PASS pilots.

Ovtšarenko, Scientific Reports, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (Scientific Reports, Nature Portfolio)

entry.title: What login patterns and grades reveal about who drops out of Korea's largest online university
entry.summary:
Researchers at Hanyang Cyber University in Seoul analysed 144,540 student instances recorded between 2018 and 2022, testing logistic regression, XGBoost and light gradient boosting (LGBM) models built from 128 predictors covering demographics, academic records, admissions and learning management system logs. The best LGBM model, trained on eight semesters of data, reached a ROC-AUC of 0.875 for predicting dropout, with age, residential area, occupation, GPA and LMS activity as the strongest signals, and dropout patterns differed by gender.

Why it matters here: This is a directly comparable case at national distance-education scale: a multi-year, multi-semester dataset built from routine administrative and LMS data, exactly the kind PASS aims to assemble from Wits School of Education records, and its comparison of several algorithms and predictor sets offers a benchmark for choosing models and features.

Seo, Yang, Lee and So, Heliyon, 2024 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (Heliyon, Elsevier)

entry.title: Qatar University tracks seven years of health-sciences students to see who stays, repeats or graduates
entry.summary:
Researchers at Qatar University's Health Cluster analysed data on 1,942 first-year health-professions students enrolled between 2015 and 2021 (754 Qatari women, 99 Qatari men, 876 non-Qatari women and 213 non-Qatari men) and trained an XGBoost model that reached 83 per cent accuracy on held-out test data for predicting second-year retention. First-year cumulative GPA and high-school GPA were the two strongest predictors, most students graduated from their health colleges within four to seven years, and retention dropped most for non-Qatari and male students in autumn 2020.

Why it matters here: It shows how a single-institution predictive model for retention can be built from routinely collected admissions and GPA data alone, without new data collection, a low-cost starting point PASS could mirror as it builds its first model from Wits School of Education records before adding richer variables.

Hammoudi Halat et al., BMC Medical Education, 2023 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (BMC Medical Education)

entry.title: A fairness-audited early-warning model built on Morocco's national school data system
entry.summary:
The study used anonymised records from Morocco's national Massar education information system, covering 451,852 middle school third-year students in the RSK region, to predict end-of-year pass or fail outcomes about five months before final examinations using first-semester performance data. Nine machine learning models were tested against a hard recall threshold of at least 0.85; the best-performing model, a multilayer perceptron, reached a recall of 0.867 and an AUC-PR of 0.888. An intersectional fairness audit found a persistent gap for male students in rural areas (AUC 0.935 against 0.953 to 0.966 for other groups), and a bias-mitigation step narrowed but did not remove this gap while increasing false positives.

Why it matters here: For PASS, this is a method worth borrowing directly: building a hard recall threshold and an intersectional gender-by-location fairness audit into the model itself, not as an afterthought, gives a template for checking whether a Wits School of Education model works equally well across different groups of students. It is also a rare example of an early-warning system built on a national administrative data system rather than a single institution's data, a useful contrast as PASS begins from School-level data.

El Jihaoui, Abra and Mansouri, Frontiers in Education, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, Frontiers in Education (open access)

entry.title: A machine-learning early-warning system trialled at a Nigerian state university
entry.summary:
Researchers built an early-warning system using academic, behavioural and socioeconomic data from 1,200 undergraduates at Taraba State University between 2023 and 2025, leaving 1,000 valid records after data cleaning. Comparing logistic regression with random forest, the random forest model performed best, reaching 89% accuracy and an AUC of 0.92, with attendance rate, study hours, learning-management-system engagement and parental income the most influential predictors. The authors present the system as a decision-support tool for academic administrators.

Why it matters here: This is a close African peer to PASS in scale and approach: a single Nigerian university building its own early-warning model from routinely collected academic and engagement data, much the same starting point PASS is taking with Wits School of Education data. The predictors it flags, attendance, study hours and LMS engagement, are indicators PASS could test for relevance alongside the data already available through Wits Business Intelligence Services.

Bashiru and Malgwi, Mambilla Journal of Science and the Environment, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, Taraba State University

entry.title: An open dashboard that turns retention prediction into an administrator's tool
entry.summary:
A team from Mindanao State University and De La Salle University in the Philippines built EduGuard RetainX, an analytical dashboard that combines academic performance, particularly mathematics and programming grades, admission test scores, GPA, programme and sociodemographic details such as age and sex, to forecast the likelihood that an individual student will withdraw. The dashboard is aimed at institutional decision-makers rather than researchers, and a usability evaluation using a published dashboard-evaluation checklist returned a positive score of 89%.

Why it matters here: EduGuard RetainX is a directly comparable practice piece for PASS: a retention dashboard built and evaluated by a small institutional team, with peer-reviewed evidence of its usability, published openly under a Creative Commons licence through SoftwareX, a journal designed for sharing usable research software. It offers PASS a concrete design precedent for the interface that Business Intelligence Services and the School might eventually build around the predictive model, and a model for how to publish and licence it.

Dia, Sieras, Khalid, Macatotong, Mondejar, Genotiva and Delena, SoftwareX, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article (SoftwareX), open access under CC BY 4.0

entry.title: A national body runs the analytics and the university runs the support
entry.summary:
Jisc reports that the University of Northampton has chosen its learning analytics service for the whole institution, replacing two separate systems with one, and will extend access to all students from September with full rollout at the start of the 2026 to 2027 academic year. The service combines attendance monitoring, engagement dashboards, reporting and analytics, case management and a student app in one environment. Jisc names Abertay, Bournemouth, City St George's University of London, Salford, South Wales and Suffolk among the other United Kingdom providers already using it.

Why it matters here: PASS is building models from Wits data with the University's Business Intelligence Services, so the interesting part here is the division of labour: a national body supplies the analytics platform while each university keeps the case management and the intervention. It is a live example of the shared-service option Wits could weigh against building everything in house.

Jisc, news item, 20 August 2026 · Announcement from Jisc, the United Kingdom's national body for digital services in tertiary education

entry.title: Thirty-three thousand Assam student records, and a model that explains why it flagged you
entry.summary:
Six authors led from Dibrugarh University in Assam analysed 33,627 student records from colleges affiliated to the university, covering students admitted in 2023 and 39 academic and demographic attributes. They compared regression and classification methods and then used explainable artificial intelligence techniques, including SHAP and LIME, to show which features drove each prediction. Logistic regression identified at-risk students with 98.43 per cent accuracy, 99.08 per cent precision and 97.86 per cent recall, and the most influential features were total credit points and overall semester marks, with raised dropout risk below 200 marks and 50 credit points.

Why it matters here: PASS will have to justify to staff and to students why a model flagged a particular person, and this study shows the explanation layer being built in from the start rather than added afterwards. The scale, drawn from affiliated colleges rather than one campus, is also close to the kind of multi-site data a South African faculty would need to pool.

Paul, R., Sarker, S., El Aouifi, H., Hussain, S., Baruah, A. K. and Gaftandzhieva, S., Frontiers in Education, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: Colombia costed its national dropout early-warning system and found it paid for itself
entry.summary:
The Colombian Ministry of Education launched SPADIES, the System for the Prevention and Analysis of School Dropouts in Higher Education Institutions, in 2004 to help institutions collect, analyse and visualise student data, prevent dropout and re-engage students who had already left. Using a differences-in-differences design, the study finds SPADIES lowered dropout probability by 0.7 percentage points, raised on-time graduation by 0.6 points and overall graduation by 0.4 points. The author notes that 0.7 percentage points is roughly 14,000 students, and that the system cost 4.9 million United States dollars between 2005 and 2017 at 2025 prices, about 350 dollars for each student who did not drop out.

Why it matters here: PASS is being built one faculty at a time, and this is what the same idea looks like after twenty years at national scale, with a causal design and a price tag attached. The cost per student retained is the figure a Wits business case would need, and the modest effect size is a realistic expectation to set against the accuracy numbers that prediction papers usually report.

Herrera-Prada, L. O., International Journal of Educational Development, volume 116, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, subscription access

entry.title: Random forest model identifies Peruvian university dropout risk with 87 percent accuracy
entry.summary:
Four Peruvian university researchers built a predictive framework using the knowledge discovery in databases (KDD) methodology of selection, preprocessing, transformation, data mining and interpretation to flag Latin American university students at risk of dropping out. Their random forest model reached 87% accuracy, 86% precision, 85% recall, an F1-score of 85% and a ROC AUC of 0.91, outperforming the other approaches they tested, and the authors recommend it be adopted by universities for early identification of at-risk students.

Why it matters here: Provides PASS with a recent, fully open-access Latin American benchmark for a transparent tree-based classifier reaching strong accuracy on dropout risk, a useful comparison point for the models PASS will validate on Wits School of Education data, and evidence that KDD-style data pipelines translate well across university contexts.

Andrade-Arenas, Rubio Paucar, Giraldo Retuerto and Yactayo-Arias, IAES International Journal of Artificial Intelligence (IJ-AI), 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY 4.0)

entry.title: Propensity score analysis shows a university scholarship cuts dropout odds by 40 percent
entry.summary:
Two San Diego State University statisticians compared five predictive models, lasso regression, a generalised additive model, random forest, XGBoost and a neural network, on 3,400 records of students at Portugal's Polytechnic Institute of Portalegre enrolled between 2008/09 and 2018/19. XGBoost reached the best F1-score of 0.904, with 88.2% accuracy and 94.7% precision, and random forest reached the best area under the curve at 0.935; a propensity score matching analysis then found that receiving a scholarship reduced the odds of dropping out by nearly 40%, equivalent to a 22.2 percentage point drop in dropout probability.

Why it matters here: Goes beyond prediction to intervention evidence, exactly PASS's next step of co-creating interventions with the University's Business Intelligence Services: it demonstrates a rigorous, quasi-experimental method, propensity score matching, for testing whether a specific support measure, a scholarship, actually reduces dropout once confounders are controlled for.

Romero and Liao, PLoS ONE, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: Randomised trial finds human judgement still matters inside Georgia State's advising algorithm
entry.summary:
Researchers from Princeton University, Columbia Business School and Georgia State University's own advising team analysed a randomised controlled trial of Georgia State's algorithm-assisted advising programme. They found that roughly two out of three interventions advisers made in the treatment arm were expertly targeted using context the algorithm did not have, such as students' personal circumstances, financial factors and engagement, drawn from advisers' own notes, and that different advising styles were associated with different graduation rates.

Why it matters here: A direct empirical caution for PASS as it moves from prediction to co-created interventions with Business Intelligence Services and advisers: it shows that even a mature, long-running algorithmic advising system still depends on advisers' contextual judgement, supporting a human-in-the-loop design rather than a fully automated one.

Schechtman, Brandon, Stafford, Li and Liu, arXiv preprint, 2025 (accepted for ACM EAAMO 2025) · Working paper (arXiv preprint), co-authored with Georgia State University's own advising staff, accepted for the ACM Equity and Access in Algorithms, Mechanisms and Optimization (EAAMO) 2025 conference

entry.title: Predicting late postgraduate graduation at Makerere: 500 students, 71% finishing late, and a simple logistic model that matches the ensembles
entry.summary:
A retrospective modelling study used anonymised administrative records of 500 postgraduate students registered at Makerere University between 2017 and 2023, of whom 29% graduated on time and 71% late. Random forest, XGBoost, k-nearest neighbours, logistic regression and a stacking ensemble all reached similar accuracy of about 94% to 95% and ROC-AUC between 0.94 and 0.95, with logistic regression numerically highest at 0.950 and no statistically meaningful differences between classifiers. Being employed and older age at admission were associated with delayed graduation, while a higher undergraduate grade point average reduced the likelihood of late completion; the authors argue that interpretable models can match complex ensembles on structured educational data.

Why it matters here: A direct African precedent for PASS on the postgraduate side: the same outcome (timely completion), the same reliance on anonymised institutional records, and a finding that a transparent model performs as well as ensembles, which supports the project's aim of models that advisers and Business Intelligence Services can explain.

Lubelenga, Kivunike, Chongomweru and Ahishakiye, Discover Artificial Intelligence, volume 6, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY)

entry.title: Inside the black box: student-success predictions are less accurate for racially minoritised students, and the usual bias fixes do not close the gap
entry.summary:
Using nationally representative data from the Education Longitudinal Study of 2002 and several machine learning approaches, the authors tested how accurately models built on commonly used features predict college success for different racialised groups. The models were less accurate for racially minoritised students, which the authors read as algorithmic bias inherited from historical data that captures societal injustice, including racism. They then applied leading bias-mitigation techniques and found them generally ineffective at removing the disparities in prediction outcomes and accuracy between groups. The American Educational Research Association named the paper the most outstanding article published in its journals in 2025.

Why it matters here: A caution PASS must design against from the start: accuracy has to be reported by group, not just overall, and the Wits models, trained on a South African student body with its own historical inequities, cannot assume that off-the-shelf fairness adjustments will fix disparities that the data carry.

Gándara, Anahideh, Ison and Picchiarini, AERA Open, volume 10, 2024; winner of AERA's 2025 Palmer O. Johnson Memorial Award · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY-NC); AERA award for the most outstanding article in an AERA journal

entry.title: 11,698 first-year students and 69 variables: a random-forest early-warning model in Türkiye reaches 90.2% accuracy once the first-semester average is known
entry.summary:
Researchers from three Istanbul universities and a bank's business intelligence department built an early-warning system that classifies first-year undergraduates as likely to succeed or fail by the end of the year. The dataset covered 11,698 first-year students and 69 input variables; naive Bayes, decision tree and random forest models were compared, and random forest performed best with 90.2% accuracy. Models that included the autumn-semester grade point average performed dramatically better, and the student's programme and university placement examination score were the next most important variables. The authors propose acting on the predictions from the second week of the spring semester so that support reaches students before attrition occurs.

Why it matters here: A useful comparison for the Wits School of Education data: the finding that the first-semester average dominates suggests PASS should test how early a reliable flag can be raised, and the joint authorship with a business intelligence unit mirrors the project's planned work with Wits Business Intelligence Services.

Çırak, Akıllı and Ekinci, Higher Education Quarterly, volume 78, issue 4, 2024 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Wiley)

entry.title: From risk score to recommended action: prescriptive dropout analytics for 2,500 foundation-programme entrants in Ecuador
entry.summary:
Escuela Superior Politécnica del Litoral (ESPOL) in Guayaquil built a prescriptive analytics pipeline for a computing-oriented bachelor's programme, tracking 2,500 students who entered its foundation programme between 2020 and 2024, of whom 9.1% (228) dropped out. A Random Forest classifier using 58 features drawn from foundation-stage academic, socioeconomic and connectivity data reached a ROC-AUC of 0.95 to 0.97; k-means clustering split students into three profiles with observed dropout of 0.6% (high-resource), 5.7% (intermediate) and 25.7% (vulnerable), and the authors added SHAP explanations and counterfactual recourse tools (DiCE, CARLA, Alibi) to turn each score into a specific recommended action.

Why it matters here: Goes a step beyond prediction to prescription, the direction PASS itself wants to take once its own risk model is validated: a worked example of turning a risk score into an explainable, student-specific recommendation, and a profile-based reading of risk (by resource level, not just a single score) that the Emory-Wits team could test against its own Wits School of Education data.

Quijije-Castro, Peláez and colleagues, Frontiers in Education 11 (2026), open access · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: Gradient boosting and 32 advisers: a deployed early-warning system evaluated for usability, not just accuracy
entry.summary:
Researchers at ISI Bali and Universitas Sains dan Teknologi Komputer, Semarang, built and deployed a web-based early-warning system on 1,240 student records from 2021 to 2024, combining institutional records with Moodle behavioural data such as weekly login frequency and assignment submission timing. A Gradient Boosting model, chosen after comparing four algorithms with stratified ten-fold cross-validation and SMOTE class balancing, reached 89.1% accuracy, an F1-score of 0.850 and an AUC-ROC of 0.931; 32 academic advisers then rated the deployed system on the System Usability Scale at a mean of 78.4, above-average usability.

Why it matters here: Most early-warning papers in this feed stop at model accuracy; this one also asks whether the advisers who receive the alerts find the system usable, a question PASS will face once its own model reaches Wits School of Education advisers, and the login-frequency and submission-timing predictors are simple LMS signals the project could test early.

Handayani and Priyadi, Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Information Technology (2026) · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: 143,326 anonymised records, seven cohorts: an open dropout-prediction dataset from Tecnologico de Monterrey
entry.summary:
Tecnologico de Monterrey released a curated, non-identifiable dataset of 50 variables across 143,326 records covering 121,584 high school and undergraduate students from seven admission cohorts, August to December 2014 to 2020, spanning two educational models. The variables cover sociodemographic and academic information alongside institution-specific measures such as student life, and the dataset was built specifically so other researchers can train and compare dropout-prediction models.

Why it matters here: An open, ready-to-use dataset at a scale the PASS team is unlikely to match from Wits School of Education records alone; a natural benchmark for testing whether models built on South African data generalise, or a training set to trial methods on before running them on the School's own anonymised data.

Alvarado-Uribe, Mejía-Almada, Herrera, Molontay, Hilliger, Hegde, Montemayor Gallegos, Díaz and Ceballos, Data 7(9), 119 (2022), open access, CC BY · Peer-reviewed data descriptor, open access, CC BY

entry.title: OU Analyse: weekly machine-learning risk scores for every distance student, and a decade of published evaluation
entry.summary:
OU Analyse predicts each student's risk of failing the next assignment and updates the prediction weekly for tutors and student support teams, with the aim of improving retention across the Open University. The team has published on teachers' use and perceptions three years after implementation (LAK 2023), on co-creating an equality, diversity and inclusion dashboard to address awarding gaps (BJET 2024) and on a student-facing dashboard designed with students (LAK 2025, Journal of Learning Analytics 2025).

Why it matters here: A mature, evaluated system in a distance-learning setting close to much South African provision, with an open dataset the PASS models can be benchmarked against and a research track record on how teachers actually use predictions.

The Open University, OU Analyse (Knowledge Media Institute); Herodotou et al., Journal of Learning Analytics and LAK 2023 to 2025 · Institutional system with peer-reviewed evaluations

entry.title: Siyaphumelela: a national data-for-student-success network reaching 80% of South Africa's public university students
entry.summary:
Launched in 2014, Siyaphumelela works with post-school institutions to use data to improve access, retention, progression, graduation and work-readiness. It reports 20 partner universities, 80% of public university students reached, more than 1,500 university staff trained and R338 million invested, with an annual national conference and a focus on eliminating performance gaps by race, gender and socio-economic status.

Why it matters here: The South African ecosystem PASS sits inside: the institutions, staff and data practices already built through Siyaphumelela are the natural partners and audience for the Wits models and interventions, and the network's conference is a dissemination route.

Siyaphumelela, led by Saide in partnership with The Kresge Foundation (initiative site) · National initiative, funder-backed

entry.title: GPS Advising: more than 800 alerts, every undergraduate tracked daily, advisers who act the same week
entry.summary:
Georgia State runs predictive analytics over all undergraduates with a system of more than 800 alerts; when an alert fires, an adviser intervenes. The system went live in August 2012 and in one recent academic year generated more than 55,000 adviser-student meetings about specific alerts. Since 2012 first-year fall-to-spring retention has risen by five percentage points and graduating seniors take fewer excess courses.

Why it matters here: The best-known working model of what PASS proposes: prediction is only half the design; the other half is a person with time to act on each alert. Georgia State's alert-to-adviser loop is the pattern to test with Wits Business Intelligence Services and the School's advisers.

Georgia State University, Student Success Initiatives (institutional page) · Institutional programme page
